We establish a one-to-one correspondence between (i) exchangeable sequences of random variables whose finite-dimensional distributions are minimum (or maximum) infinitely divisible and (ii) non-negative, non-decreasing, infinitely divisible stochastic processes. The exponent measure of an exchangeable minimum infinitely divisible sequence is shown to be the sum of a very simple ``drift measure'' and a mixture of product probability measures, which uniquely corresponds to the L 'evy measure of a non-negative and non-decreasing infinitely divisible process. The latter is shown to be supported on non-negative and non-decreasing functions. In probabilistic terms, the aforementioned infinitely divisible process is equal to the conditional cumulative hazard process associated with the exchangeable sequence of random variables with minimum (or maximum) infinitely divisible marginals. Our results provide an analytic umbrella which embeds the de Finetti subfamilies of many interesting classes of multivariate distributions, such as exogenous shock models, exponential and geometric laws with lack-of-memory property, min-stable multivariate exponential and extreme-value distributions, as well as reciprocal Archimedean copulas with completely monotone generator and Archimedean copulas with log-completely monotone generator.

A new calibration method for H-fs-TALIF is proposed, and the ratio of two-photon absorption cross-sections, $ sigma^{(2)}$, for atomic hydrogen (H) and krypton (Kr) is determined for the broadband emission of a femtosecond laser system. The estimated ratio of the two-photon absorption cross-sections for H and Kr is $ sigma^{(2)}$ for H and Kr $ sigma^{(2)}$(Kr)/$ sigma^{(2)}$(H) = $0.027 pm 20$%, which is nearly twenty times lower than values previously obtained with narrowband nanosecond lasers. This discrepancy highlights the need for independent calibration of TALIF measurements for a specific laser pulsewidth range.

Recovering images from optical interferometric observations is one of the major challenges in the field. Unlike the case of observations at radio wavelengths, in the optical the atmospheric turbulence changes the phases on a very short time scale, which results in corrupted phase measurements. In order to overcome these limitations, several groups developed image reconstruction techniques based only on squared visibility and closure phase information, which are unaffected by atmospheric turbulence. We present the results of two techniques used by our group, which employed coherently integrated data from the Navy Prototype Optical Interferometer. Based on these techniques we were able to recover complex visibilities for several sources and image them using standard radio imaging software. We describe these techniques, the corrections applied to the data, present the images of a few sources, and discuss the implications of these results.

We embed spherical Rindler space -- a geometry with a spherical hole in its center -- in asymptotically AdS spacetime and show that it carries a gravitational entropy proportional to the area of the hole. Spherical AdS-Rindler space is holographically dual to an ultraviolet sector of the boundary field theory given by restriction to a strip of finite duration in time. Because measurements have finite durations, local observers in the field theory can only access information about bounded spatial regions. We propose a notion of Residual Entropy that captures uncertainty about the state of a system left by the collection of local, finite-time observables. For two-dimensional conformal field theories we use holography and the strong subadditivity of entanglement to propose a formula for Residual Entropy and show that it precisely reproduces the areas of circular holes in AdS3. Extending the notion to field theories on strips with variable durations in time, we show more generally that Residual Entropy computes the areas of all closed, inhomogenous curves on a spatial slice of AdS3. We discuss the extension to higher dimensional field theories, the relation of Residual Entropy to entanglement between scales, and some implications for the emergence of space from the RG flow of entangled field theories.

In this paper, we find a family $SL^{n,m}$, in any arbitrary dimensions, of cohomologically rigid solvable Lie superalgebras with nilradical the model filiform Lie superalgebra $L^{n,m}$. Moreover, we exhibit a family of cohomologically rigid solvable Lie superalgebras with nilradical the model nilpotent Lie superalgebra of generic characteristic sequence. Both cases correspond to solvable Lie superalgebras of maximal dimension for a given nilradical. Contrariwise, we will show that the family of Lie superalgebras $SL^{n,m}$ can be deformed if defined over a field of odd characteristic.

Existences of vector-like quarks (VLQs) are predicted in many new physics scenarios beyond the Standard Model (SM). We study the possibility of detecting the vector-like bottom quark (VLQ-$B$) being the $SU(2)$ singlet with electric charge $-1/3$ at the Large Hadron Electron Collider (LHeC) in a model-independent framework. The decay properties and single production of VLQ-$B$ at the LHeC are explored. Three types of signatures are investigated. By carrying out a fast simulation for the signals and the corresponding backgrounds, the signal significances are obtained. Our numerical results show that detecting of VLQ-$B$ via the semileptonic channel is better than via the fully hadronic or leptonic channel.

The pharmacopeia used by physicians and lay people in medieval Europe has largely been dismissed as placebo or superstition. While we now recognise that some of the materia medica used by medieval physicians could have had useful biological properties, research in this area is limited by the labour-intensive process of searching and interpreting historical medical texts. Here, we demonstrate the potential power of turning medieval medical texts into contextualised electronic databases amenable to exploration by algorithm. We use established methodologies from network science to reveal statistically significant patterns in ingredient selection and usage in a key text, the fifteenth-century Lylye of Medicynes, focusing on remedies to treat symptoms of microbial infection. We discuss the potential that these patterns reflect rational medical decisions. In providing a worked example of data-driven textual analysis, we demonstrate the potential of this approach to encourage interdisciplinary collaboration and to shine a new light on the ethnopharmacology of historical medical texts.

Attosecond streaking of atomic photoemission holds the promise to provide unprecedented information on the release time of the photoelectron. We show that attosecond streaking phase shifts indeed contain timing (or spectral phase) information associated with the Eisenbud-Wigner-Smith time delay matrix of quantum scattering. However, this is only accessible if the influence of the streaking infrared (IR) field on the emission process is properly accounted for. The IR probe field can strongly modify the observed streaking phase shift. We show that the part of the phase shift ( time shift ) due to the interaction between the outgoing electron and the combined Coulomb and IR laser fields can be described classically. By contrast, the strong initial-state dependence of the streaking phase shift is only revealed through the solution of the time-dependent Schr  odinger equation in its full dimensionality. We find a time delay between the hydrogenic 2s and 2p initial states in He+ exceeding 20as for a wide range of IR intensities and XUV energies.

The radial drift and diffusion of dust particles in protoplanetary disks affect both the opacity and temperature of such disks as well as the location and timing of planetesimal formation. In this paper, we present results of numerical simulations of particle-gas dynamics in protoplanetary disks that include dust grains with various size distributions. We consider three scenarios in terms of particle size ranges, one where the Stokes number $ tau_{ rm{s}} = 10^{-1} - 10^0$, one where $ tau_{ rm{s}} = 10^{-4} - 10^{-1}$ and finally one where $ tau_{ rm{s}} = 10^{-3} - 10^{0}$. Moreover, we consider both discrete and continuous distributions in particle size. In accordance with previous works we find in our multi-species simulations that different particle sizes interact via the gas and as a result their dynamics changes compared to the single-species case. The larger species trigger the streaming instability and create turbulence that drives the diffusion of the solid materials. We measure the radial equilibrium velocity of the system and find that the radial drift velocity of the large particles is reduced in the multi-species simulations and that the small particle species move on average outwards. We also vary the steepness of the size distribution, such that the exponent of the solid number density distribution, $ rm{d} it{N}/ rm{d} it{a}  propto  it{a^{-q}}$, is either $q = 3$ or $q = 4$. We measure the scale height of the particles and observe that small grains are stirred up well above the sedimented midplane layer where the large particles reside. Our measured diffusion and drift parameters can be used in coagulation models for planet formation as well as to understand relative mixing of the components of primitive meteorites (matrix, chondrules and CAIs) prior to inclusion in their parent bodies.

We report the identification of LP 400-22 (WD 2234+222) as a very low-mass and high-velocity white dwarf. The ultraviolet GALEX and optical photometric colors and a spectral line analysis of LP 400-22 show this star to have an effective temperature of 11080+/-140 K and a surface gravity of log g = 6.32+/-0.08. Therefore, this is a helium core white dwarf with a mass of 0.17 M_solar. The tangential velocity of this white dwarf is 414+/-43 km/s, making it one of the fastest moving white dwarfs known. We discuss probable evolutionary scenarios for this remarkable object.

As in our previous work [1] we address the problem to determine the splitting of the normal bundle of rational curves. With apolarity theory we are able to characterize some particular subvarieties in some Hilbert scheme of rational curves, defined by the splitting type of the normal bundle and the restricted tangent bundle.

We describe two ground based observing campaigns aimed at building a grid of approximately 200 spectrophotometric standard stars (SPSS), with an internal ~1% precision and tied to Vega within ~3%, for the absolute flux calibration of data gathered by Gaia, the ESA astrometric mission. The criteria for the selection and a list of candidates are presented, together with a description of the survey strategy and the adopted data analysis methods. We also discuss a short list of notable rejected SPSS candidates and difficult cases, based on identification problems, literature discordant data, visual companions, and variability. In fact, all candidates are also monitored for constancy (within  pm5 mmag, approximately). In particular, we report on a CALSPEC standard, 1740346, that we found to be a delta Scuti variable during our short-term monitoring (1-2 h) campaign.

Fueled by both advances in robust optimization theory and applications of reinforcement learning, robust Markov Decision Processes (RMDPs) have gained increasing attention, due to their powerful capability for sequential decision-making under uncertainty. This review provides an in-depth overview of the evolution and advances in RMDPs formulations, particularly in ambiguity modeling, and classifies these methods for representing uncertainty into three principal approaches: parametric, moment-based, and discrepancy-based, elaborating the trade-offs among the alternative representations. Meanwhile, the review delves into the rectangular assumptions, which guarantee the tractability of RMDPs yet are noted for their conservatism. The review summarizes three popular rectangular conditions and develops a new proof to attest to the NP-hardness of non-rectangular RMDPs. Out of the traditional RMDPs scope, recent efforts without conventional rectangular assumptions and new fashions within the RMDPs community are also reviewed. These studies foster the development of more flexible and practical modeling frameworks and enhance the adaptability and performance of RMDPs.

At high-energies the gluon-gluon fusion is the dominant mechanism of $c  bar c$ production. This process was calculated in the NLO collinear as well as in the k$_t$-factorization approaches in the past. We show that the present knowledge of gluon distributions does not allow to make a precise predictions for $c  bar c$ production at LHC, in particular at forward rapidities. In this paper we study production of $c  bar c$ pairs including several subleading mechanisms. This includes: $gg  to Q  bar Q$, $ gamma g  to Q  bar Q$, $g  gamma  to Q  bar Q$, $ gamma  gamma  to Q  bar Q$. In this context we use MRST-QED parton distributions which include photon as a parton in the proton as well as elastic photon distributions calculated in the equivalent photon approximation. We present distributions in the $c$ quark ($ bar c$ antiquark) rapidity and transverse momenta and compare them to the dominant gluon-gluon fusion contribution. We discuss also inclusive single and central diffractive processes using diffractive parton distribution found from the analysis of HERA diffractive data. As in the previous case we present distribution in $c$ ($ bar c$) rapidity and transverse momentum. Finally we present results for exclusive central diffractive mechanism discussed recently in the literature. We show corresponding differential distributions and compare them with corresponding distributions for single and central diffractive components.

Quantum steering, an intermediate quantum correlation lying between entanglement and nonlocality, has emerged as a critical quantum resource for a variety of quantum information processing tasks such as quantum key distribution and true randomness generation. The ability to detect and quantify quantum steering is crucial for these applications. Semi-definite programming (SDP) has proven to be a valuable tool to quantify quantum steering. However, the challenge lies in the fact that the optimal measurement strategy is not priori known, making it time-consuming to compute the steerable measure for any given quantum state. Furthermore, the utilization of SDP requires full information of the quantum state, necessitating quantum state tomography, which can be complex and resource-consuming. In this work, we utilize the semi-supervised self-training model to estimate the steerable weight, a pivotal measure of quantum steering. The model can be trained using a limited amount of labeled data, thus reducing the time for labeling. The features are constructed by the probabilities derived by performing three sets of projective measurements under arbitrary local unitary transformations on the target states, circumventing the need for quantum tomography. The model demonstrates robust generalization capabilities and can achieve high levels of precision with limited resources.

A description is provided of the software algorithms developed for the CMS tracker both for reconstructing charged-particle trajectories in proton-proton interactions and for using the resulting tracks to estimate the positions of the LHC luminous region and individual primary-interaction vertices. Despite the very hostile environment at the LHC, the performance obtained with these algorithms is found to be excellent. For ttbar events under typical 2011 pileup conditions, the average track-reconstruction efficiency for promptly-produced charged particles with transverse momenta of pt > 0.9 GeV is 94% for pseudorapidities of abs(eta) < 0.9 and 85% for 0.9 < abs(eta) < 2.5. The inefficiency is caused mainly by hadrons that undergo nuclear interactions in the tracker material. For isolated muons, the corresponding efficiencies are essentially 100%. For isolated muons of pt = 100 GeV emitted at abs(eta) < 1.4, the resolutions are approximately 2.8% in pt, and respectively, 10 microns and 30 microns in the transverse and longitudinal impact parameters. The position resolution achieved for reconstructed primary vertices that correspond to interesting pp collisions is 10-12 microns in each of the three spatial dimensions. The tracking and vertexing software is fast and flexible, and easily adaptable to other functions, such as fast tracking for the trigger, or dedicated tracking for electrons that takes into account bremsstrahlung.

In smooth and convex multiobjective optimization problems the set of Pareto optima is diffeomorphic to an $m-1$ dimensional simplex, where $m$ is the number of objective functions. The vertices of the simplex are the optima of the individual functions and the $(k-1)$-dimensional facets are the Pareto optimal set of $k$ functions subproblems. Such a hierarchy of submanifolds is a geometrical object called stratification and the union of such manifolds, in this case the set of Pareto optima, is called a stratified set. We discuss how these geometrical structures generalize in the non convex cases, we survey the known results and deduce possible suggestions for the design of dedicated optimization strategies.

In recent years, large language models (LLMs), such as ChatGPT, have been pivotal in advancing various artificial intelligence applications, including natural language processing and software engineering. A promising yet underexplored area is utilizing LLMs in software testing, particularly in black-box testing. This paper explores the test cases devised by ChatGPT in comparison to those created by human participants. In this study, ChatGPT (GPT-4) and four participants each created black-box test cases for three applications based on specifications written by the authors. The goal was to evaluate the real-world applicability of the proposed test cases, identify potential shortcomings, and comprehend how ChatGPT could enhance human testing strategies. ChatGPT can generate test cases that generally match or slightly surpass those created by human participants in terms of test viewpoint coverage. Additionally, our experiments demonstrated that when ChatGPT cooperates with humans, it can cover considerably more test viewpoints than each can achieve alone, suggesting that collaboration between humans and ChatGPT may be more effective than human pairs working together. Nevertheless, we noticed that the test cases generated by ChatGPT have certain issues that require addressing before use.

In a previous work of the first authors, a non-holonomic model, generalising the micromorphic models and allowing for curvature (disclinations) to arise from the kinematic values, was presented. In the present paper, a generalisation of the classical models of Euler-Bernoulli and Timoshenko bending beams based on the mentioned work is proposed. The former is still composed of only one unidimensional scalar field, while the later introduces a third unidimensional scalar field, correcting the second order terms. The generalised Euler-Bernoulli beam is then shown to exhibit curvature (i.e. disclinations) linked to a third order derivative of the displacement, but no torsion (dislocations). Parallelly, the generalised Timoshenko beam is shown to exhibit both curvature and torsion, where the former is linked to the non-holonomy introduced in the generalisation. Lastly, using variational calculus, asymptotic values for the value taken by the curvature in static equilibrium are obtained when the second order contribution becomes negligible; along with an equation for the torsion in the generalised Timoshenko beam.

We consider a Sklyanin algebra S with 3 generators, which is the quadratic algebra over a field k with three generators x,y,z given by three relations pxy+qyx+rzz=0, pyz+qzy+rxx=0 and pzx+qxz+ryy=0, where p,q,r are parameters from the fileld k. This class of algebras enjoyed much of attention, in particular, using tools from algebraic geometry, Feigin & Odesskii, and Artin, Tate & Van den Berg, showed that if at least two of the parameters p, q and r are non-zero and at least two of three numbers p^3,q^3 and r^3 are distinct, then S is Koszul and has the same Hilbert series as the algebra of commutative polynomials in three variables. It became commonly accepted, that it is impossible to achieve the same objective by purely algebraic and combinatorial means, like the Groebner basis technique. The main purpose of this paper is to trace combinatorial meaning of the properties of Sklyanin algebras, such as Koszulity, PBW, PHS, Calabi-Yau, and to give a new constructive proof of the above facts due to Artin, Tate and Van den Bergh.   Further, we study a wider class of Sklyanin algebras, namely the situation when all parameters of relations could be different. This class called generalized Sklyanin algebras. We classify up to isomorphism genralized Sklyanin algebras with polynomial Hilbert series. We show that generalized Slyanin algebras in general position have the Golod-Shafarevich Hilbert series (with exception of the case of the field with two elements).

In this paper, we review observational aspects of three common small-scale energetic events in the solar transition region (TR), namely: TR explosive events, ultraviolet bursts and jets. These events are defined in either (both) spectral or (and) imaging data. The development of multiple instruments capable of observing the TR has allowed researchers to gain numerous insights into these phenomena in recent years. These events have provided a proxy to study how mass and energy are transported between the solar chromosphere and the corona. As the physical mechanisms responsible for these small-scale events might be similar to the mechanisms responsible for large-scale phenomena, such as flares and coronal mass ejections, analysis of these events could also help our understanding of the solar atmosphere from small to large scales. The observations of these small-scale energetic events demonstrate that the TR is extremely dynamic and is a crucial layer in the solar atmosphere between the chromosphere and the corona.

Wearable egocentric cameras and machine learning have the potential to provide clinicians with a more nuanced understanding of patient hand use at home after stroke and spinal cord injury (SCI). However, they require detailed contextual information (i.e., activities and object interactions) to effectively interpret metrics and meaningfully guide therapy planning. We demonstrate that an object-centric approach, focusing on what objects patients interact with rather than how they move, can effectively recognize Activities of Daily Living (ADL) in real-world rehabilitation settings. We evaluated our models on a complex dataset collected in the wild comprising 2261 minutes of egocentric video from 16 participants with impaired hand function. By leveraging pre-trained object detection and hand-object interaction models, our system achieves robust performance across different impairment levels and environments, with our best model achieving a mean weighted F1-score of 0.78 +/- 0.12 and maintaining an F1-score > 0.5 for all participants using leave-one-subject-out cross validation. Through qualitative analysis, we observe that this approach generates clinically interpretable information about functional object use while being robust to patient-specific movement variations, making it particularly suitable for rehabilitation contexts with prevalent upper limb impairment.

We analytically prove that the existence of the delta-function singularity in the chirally-odd twist-3 distribution $e(x)$ of the nucleon is inseparably connected with the nonvanishing quark condensate as a signal of the spontaneous chiral symmetry breaking of the QCD vacuum. This singularity in $e(x)$, which would be observed as a sizable violation of the 1st moment sum rule, is then interpreted as giving a very rare case that the nontrivial vacuum structure of QCD manifests in an observable of a localized QCD excitation, i.e. the nucleon.

Functional data analysis has been extensively conducted. In this study, we consider a partially functional model, under which some covariates are scalars and have linear effects, while some other variables are functional and have unspecified nonlinear effects. Significantly advancing from the existing literature, we consider a model with interactions between the functional and scalar covariates. To accommodate long-tailed error distributions which are not uncommon in data analysis, we adopt the quantile technique for estimation. To achieve more interpretable estimation, and to accommodate many practical settings, we assume that the functional covariate effects are locally sparse (that is, there exist subregions on which the effects are exactly zero), which naturally leads to a variable/model selection problem. We propose respecting the  main effect, interaction  hierarchy, which postulates that if a subregion has a nonzero effect in an interaction term, then its effect has to be nonzero in the corresponding main functional effect. For estimation, identification of local sparsity, and respect of the hierarchy, we propose a penalization approach. An effective computational algorithm is developed, and the consistency properties are rigorously established under mild regularity conditions. Simulation shows the practical effectiveness of the proposed approach. The analysis of the Tecator data further demonstrates its practical applicability. Overall, this study can deliver a novel and practically useful model and a statistically and numerically satisfactory estimation approach.

A commonly used technique for managing AI complexity in real-time strategy (RTS) games is to use action and/or state abstractions. High-level abstractions can often lead to good strategic decision making, but tactical decision quality may suffer due to lost details. A competing method is to sample the search space which often leads to good tactical performance in simple scenarios, but poor high-level planning.   We propose to use a deep convolutional neural network (CNN) to select among a limited set of abstract action choices, and to utilize the remaining computation time for game tree search to improve low level tactics. The CNN is trained by supervised learning on game states labelled by Puppet Search, a strategic search algorithm that uses action abstractions. The network is then used to select a script --- an abstract action --- to produce low level actions for all units. Subsequently, the game tree search algorithm improves the tactical actions of a subset of units using a limited view of the game state only considering units close to opponent units.   Experiments in the microRTS game show that the combined algorithm results in higher win-rates than either of its two independent components and other state-of-the-art microRTS agents.   To the best of our knowledge, this is the first successful application of a convolutional network to play a full RTS game on standard game maps, as previous work has focused on sub-problems, such as combat, or on very small maps.

Tool learning has emerged as a promising direction by extending Large Language Models' (LLMs) capabilities with external tools. Existing tool learning studies primarily focus on the general-purpose tool-use capability, which addresses explicit user requirements in instructions. However, they overlook the importance of personalized tool-use capability, leading to an inability to handle implicit user preferences. To address the limitation, we first formulate the task of personalized tool learning, which integrates user's interaction history towards personalized tool usage. To fill the gap of missing benchmarks, we construct PEToolBench, featuring diverse user preferences reflected in interaction history under three distinct personalized settings, and encompassing a wide range of tool-use scenarios. Moreover, we propose a framework PEToolLLaMA to adapt LLMs to the personalized tool learning task, which is trained through supervised fine-tuning and direct preference optimization. Extensive experiments on PEToolBench demonstrate the superiority of PEToolLLaMA over existing LLMs.

Renewable energy sources and further electrificationof energy consumption are key enablers for decreasing green-house gas emissions, but also introduce increased complexitywithin the electric power system. The increased availability ofautomation, information and communication technology, andintelligent solutions for system operation have transformed thepower system into a smart grid. In order to support thedevelopment process of smart grid solutions on the system level,testing has to be done in a holistic manner, covering the multi-domain aspect of such complex systems. This paper introducesthe concept of holistic power system testing and discuss first stepstowards a corresponding methodology that is being developed inthe European ERIGrid research infrastructure project.

We propose a new procedure for parton-to-hadron fragmentation in proton-proton collisions. The hadronization is considered in the parton-parton center-of-mass system and hadrons are assumed to be emitted in the direction of outgoing partons in that frame and then their four-momenta are transformed to the overall center-of-mass system using relevant Lorentz transformations and appropriate distributions are constructed. For heavy hadron production the energy-momentum condition is imposed. In many cases our procedure disagrees with the commonly used rule that rapidity of produced hadron is the same as rapidity of the parent parton. We illustrate the newly proposed scheme for production of $D$ mesons, $ Lambda_c$ baryon and $ eta_c$ quarkonium in leading-order approach to parton production. The transverse momentum, rapidity and Feynman-$x_F$ distributions are shown. We consider $c  to D$ and $g  to D$ as well as $c  to  eta_c$ and $g  to  eta_c$ hadronization processes. The resulting rapidity distributions are much narrower than those obtained in the traditional approach with parton-hadron rapidity equivalence. This has consequences both for mid- and forward rapidities and could have consequences for high-energy neutrino production in the Earth's atmosphere. We discuss also $c  to  Lambda_c^+$ and $b  to  Lambda_c^+$ fragmentation and find that the second mechanism could be partly responsible for the enhanced production of $ Lambda_c^{ pm}$ observed recently by the ALICE collaboration.

Robust and generalized tool manipulation requires an understanding of the properties and affordances of different tools. We investigate whether linguistic information about a tool (e.g., its geometry, common uses) can help control policies adapt faster to new tools for a given task. We obtain diverse descriptions of various tools in natural language and use pre-trained language models to generate their feature representations. We then perform language-conditioned meta-learning to learn policies that can efficiently adapt to new tools given their corresponding text descriptions. Our results demonstrate that combining linguistic information and meta-learning significantly accelerates tool learning in several manipulation tasks including pushing, lifting, sweeping, and hammering.

The dynamics of two-level systems in time-dependent backgrounds is under consideration. We present some new exact solutions in special backgrounds decaying in time. On the other hand, following ideas of Feynman, Vernon and Hellwarth, we discuss in detail the possibility to reduce the quantum dynamics to a classical Hamiltonian system. This, in particular, opens the possibility to directly apply powerful methods of classical mechanics (e.g. KAM methods) to study the quantum system. Following such an approach, we draw conclusions of relevance for ``quantum chaos'' when the external background is periodic or quasi-periodic in time.

We find an exact solution of the equations of motion of a two-field cosmological model, which realizes multi-field dark energy. The latter is characterized by field-space trajectories with turning rates that are always large. Mechanical defects in real situations affect observation values and cause abnormalities in multivariate time series, such as sensor values or network data. To perceive abnormalities in such data, it is crucial to understand the temporal context and interrelation between variables simultaneously. The anomaly detection task for time series, especially for unlabeled data, has been a challenging problem, and we address it by applying a suitable data degradation scheme to self-supervised model training. We define four types of synthetic outliers and propose the degradation scheme in which a portion of input data is replaced with one of the synthetic outliers. Inspired by the self-attention mechanism, we design a Transformer-based architecture to recognize the temporal context and detect unnatural sequences with high efficiency. Our model converts multivariate data points into temporal representations with relative position bias and yields anomaly scores from these representations. Our method, AnomalyBERT, shows a great capability of detecting anomalies contained in complex time series and surpasses previous state-of-the-art methods on five real-world benchmarks. Our code is available at https://github.com/Jhryu30/AnomalyBERT.

The increasing demand for controllable outputs in text-to-image generation has spurred advancements in multi-instance generation (MIG), allowing users to define both instance layouts and attributes. However, unlike image-conditional generation methods such as ControlNet, MIG techniques have not been widely adopted in state-of-the-art models like SD2 and SDXL, primarily due to the challenge of building robust renderers that simultaneously handle instance positioning and attribute rendering. In this paper, we introduce Depth-Driven Decoupled Instance Synthesis (3DIS), a novel framework that decouples the MIG process into two stages: (i) generating a coarse scene depth map for accurate instance positioning and scene composition, and (ii) rendering fine-grained attributes using pre-trained ControlNet on any foundational model, without additional training. Our 3DIS framework integrates a custom adapter into LDM3D for precise depth-based layouts and employs a finetuning-free method for enhanced instance-level attribute rendering. Extensive experiments on COCO-Position and COCO-MIG benchmarks demonstrate that 3DIS significantly outperforms existing methods in both layout precision and attribute rendering. Notably, 3DIS offers seamless compatibility with diverse foundational models, providing a robust, adaptable solution for advanced multi-instance generation. The code is available at: https://github.com/limuloo/3DIS.

Visual cryptography is a method that involves encrypting a secret message or image into multiple shares, such that the individual shares do not reveal any information about the original content. In this paper, a novel technique using a (2, 2) visual cryptographic share has been introduced.

The spin-$\frac{1}{2}$ Heisenberg antiferromagnet on the Kagomé lattice is a system of interacting spins arranged in a specific geometric pattern that exhibits unique magnetic properties. This information is crucial for understanding the phase transitions and magnetic ordering that occur in the system as it is cooled.

Additionally, we also calculate the structure factor of the Kagomé lattice, which provides information about the spatial arrangement of spins in the system. The structure factor is a powerful tool for studying the magnetic properties of the system, as it allows us to analyze the distribution of spin correlations and detect any patterns or symmetries that may exist.

By combining the information from the high-temperature series for the specific heat and the structure factor, we can paint a more complete picture of the behavior of the spin-$\frac{1}{2}$ Heisenberg antiferromagnet on the Kagomé lattice. The critical dynamics of cortical neurons have garnered significant attention and research focus in the last decade. Neuronal avalanches, which are spontaneous bursts of activity that spread through interconnected networks of neurons, have emerged as a crucial phenomenon for understanding the criticality of such neural systems. 

Experimental studies involving neural recordings have provided valuable insights into how these avalanches propagate and the role they play in information processing within the brain. Theoretical models have also been developed to simulate and explain the underlying mechanisms of neuronal avalanches and their implications for criticality.

One of the key findings from studying neuronal avalanches is that they exhibit a power law distribution of sizes, which is characteristic of critical systems. This scale-free behavior suggests that cortical neurons operate near a critical state, allowing for optimal information processing capabilities and adaptability to different stimuli. 

Furthermore, the research on cortical neuron dynamics has led to discoveries about the interconnected nature of neural networks and how they self-organize to achieve a balance between stability and flexibility. By existing at the edge of chaos, cortical neurons are able to respond dynamically to changes in their environment while maintaining overall stability.

Overall, the study of critical dynamics in cortical neurons through neuronal avalanches has uncovered fundamental principles about how the brain processes information and adapts to its surroundings. These findings have implications for understanding various neurological disorders and designing more efficient artificial neural networks.

SDFT is a powerful theoretical framework used to describe the electronic structure and magnetic properties of materials with noncollinear spins. In this theory, the Kohn-Sham equations include both the usual exchange-correlation scalar potentials that account for electron-electron interactions, as well as additional terms that incorporate the effects of magnetic fields on the spin degrees of freedom. 

The inclusion of magnetic fields in the Kohn-Sham system is crucial for accurately modeling the behavior of noncollinear magnetic materials, where the spins of neighboring atoms or molecules can be oriented in arbitrary directions relative to each other. These materials exhibit complex magnetic structures that cannot be captured within the traditional collinear approximation, making SDFT essential for understanding their unique properties.

By solving the Kohn-Sham equations within the framework of SDFT, researchers can investigate a wide range of magnetic phenomena, such as spin spirals, magnetic domain walls, and skyrmions, which play a crucial role in modern spintronics and magnetic storage technologies. Furthermore, SDFT allows for a detailed analysis of the energetics and stability of magnetic configurations, providing valuable insights into the mechanisms governing magnetic phase transitions and the emergence of novel magnetic states.

Overall, the incorporation of magnetic fields into the Kohn-Sham system within SDFT offers a comprehensive approach to studying noncollinear magnetic materials, leading to a deeper understanding of their magnetic properties and potential applications in advanced technologies.

The remarkable properties of graphene, a single layer of carbon atoms arranged in a hexagonal lattice, have made it a fascinating material for scientific research and technological applications. One of the most intriguing aspects of graphene is its ability to be doped, or intentionally introduced with impurities, in order to modify its electronic properties.

A recent experimental study has pushed the boundaries of graphene doping by demonstrating that it can be doped to beyond the Van Hove singularity. The Van Hove singularity is a critical point in the electronic band structure of materials where the density of states diverges, leading to unique electronic behaviors. By doping graphene beyond this singularity, researchers have unlocked new possibilities for manipulating its electronic properties.

This breakthrough has significant implications for the development of next-generation electronic devices, as it opens up new avenues for controlling the conductivity and band structure of graphene. By precisely doping graphene beyond the Van Hove singularity, researchers can tailor its electronic properties to suit specific applications, such as high-speed transistors, sensors, and energy storage devices.

Overall, this experimental discovery represents a major advancement in the field of graphene research and highlights the immense potential of this two-dimensional material for future technological innovations. As scientists continue to explore the vast possibilities of graphene doping, we can expect to see even more exciting breakthroughs that push the boundaries of what is possible with this remarkable material.

Gamma-ray bursts are some of the most powerful and energetic events in the universe, releasing intense flashes of gamma-ray radiation. The light curves of these bursts often exhibit complex structures, including time-reversed and stretched residuals that have puzzled researchers for some time. In an effort to provide a clearer understanding of these phenomena, we have developed a simple model that can elucidate the origins of these unique features.

Our model aims to explain the time-reversed and stretched residuals observed in GRB pulse light curves by considering the complex interactions and dynamics within the burst itself. By taking into account factors such as the geometry of the emitting region, the distribution of energy within the burst, and the effects of relativistic motion, we can simulate the observed light curves and identify the mechanisms responsible for the anomalous behavior.

Through our model, we have been able to show how the emission properties of the burst, combined with the effects of time dilation and Doppler shifting, can lead to the distinctive features seen in GRB pulse light curves. By incorporating these factors into our analysis, we can gain insights into the underlying physics of these extreme events and further our understanding of the processes involved in the generation of gamma-ray bursts.

Overall, our simple model offers a valuable framework for interpreting the time-reversed and stretched residuals in GRB pulse light curves, shedding light on the intricate dynamics at play during these powerful cosmic events. This research has the potential to deepen our knowledge of gamma-ray bursts and contribute to ongoing efforts to unravel the mysteries of the universe.

Neutrinoless double-beta decay is a rare process that, if observed, would provide crucial insights into the nature of neutrinos, specifically whether they are Majorana particles and possess their own antiparticle. The decay involves the simultaneous conversion of two neutrons into two protons, with the emission of two electrons but no neutrinos. This implies a violation of lepton number conservation and neutrinoless double-beta decay is a key probe for new physics beyond the Standard Model.

Experimental efforts focusing on the isotope Ge-76 have seen significant progress in recent years. Ge-76 is an attractive candidate for neutrinoless double-beta decay experiments due to its high natural abundance and high Q-value, making it an optimal choice for the detection of this rare process. The GERDA (GERmanium Detector Array) experiment, based in the Gran Sasso National Laboratory in Italy, is one such experiment that has been instrumental in advancing this research field. By using germanium crystals enriched in Ge-76, GERDA has been able to set stringent limits on the half-life of neutrinoless double-beta decay.

Detailed analysis of the physics potential of Ge-76 based experiments is essential for optimizing experimental design and maximizing sensitivity to neutrinoless double-beta decay. The insights gained from these analyses will not only aid in the search for this elusive process but also contribute towards a deeper understanding of the fundamental properties of neutrinos and potential extensions to the Standard Model of particle physics.

In linearized continuum elasticity, the behavior of elastic strain around a straight dislocation line has been extensively studied. It is found that the elastic strain surrounding a dislocation decays as $O(r^{-1})$, where $r$ represents the distance from the dislocation core.

This decay in elastic strain with distance from the dislocation core is a fundamental aspect of dislocation theory in solid mechanics. The $r^{-1}$ dependence signifies that the strain field diminishes as the distance from the dislocation increases. This behavior is crucial for understanding the mechanical properties of materials, as dislocations play a significant role in determining a material's strength and ductility.

The linearized continuum elasticity approach provides a simplified way to analyze the behavior of dislocations in materials. By considering the elastic properties of the material and the geometry of the dislocation, researchers can predict how the strain field will evolve around the dislocation.

Furthermore, the decay of elastic strain with distance is not only important for understanding the behavior of individual dislocations but also for studying the interactions between multiple dislocations. The $r^{-1}$ decay reflects the long-range nature of dislocation interactions, which can influence the overall mechanical response of a material.

Overall, the $r^{-1}$ decay of elastic strain around a dislocation line is a key concept in solid mechanics that aids in understanding the complex behavior of materials under stress.

When comparing isotropic solids and fluids under different conditions of imposed volume or pressure, we are able to discern the intricate interplay between their instantaneous pressure and its ideal and excess contributions. Isotropic solids exhibit a high degree of structural order at the molecular level, with tightly packed molecules forming a rigid lattice structure. On the other hand, fluids have molecules that are more loosely arranged and free to move around. 

By studying the correlations of pressure in these two types of materials, we can gain insights into their thermodynamic behavior and physical properties. When pressure is imposed on an isotropic solid, its molecules are unable to move freely, leading to an increase in pressure as the volume decreases. This is in contrast to fluids, where molecules can easily move and adjust to changes in volume without a significant increase in pressure.

The ideal contribution to pressure in both solids and fluids arises from the movement of molecules and their interactions in an idealized, perfectly ordered system. The excess contribution, on the other hand, accounts for deviations from this ideal behavior due to factors such as molecular size, shape, and interactions.

By analyzing these contributions under different conditions, researchers can develop a deeper understanding of the thermodynamic properties of isotropic solids and fluids. This knowledge can have implications for a wide range of applications, from materials science to chemical engineering.

However, in the long-range Ising model, spins interact not only with their nearest neighbors but also with spins located further away. This introduces a new level of complexity to the system and can lead to interesting phenomena not observed in the short-range version of the model.

One of the key factors that influence the behavior of the long-range Ising model is the range of the interactions. The strength and range of these interactions can dramatically affect the phase transitions and critical behavior of the system. By studying the model in two dimensions, we can investigate how the interplay between long-range interactions and dimensionality impacts the magnetic properties of the system.

Our research aims to explore the phase diagram of the long-range Ising model in two dimensions and understand how it differs from the short-range version. By using numerical simulations and theoretical analysis, we hope to uncover new insights into the behavior of magnetic materials with long-range interactions, contributing to the broader understanding of complex systems in statistical physics.

The Abelian-Higgs model in one spatial dimension and time (1+1D) on a lattice is a widely studied theoretical model in the field of condensed matter physics. This model describes the behavior of a complex scalar field coupled to a gauge field, and it has been used to study various phenomena such as superconductivity and phase transitions.

To determine the phase diagram of the Abelian-Higgs model in 1+1D on a lattice, we need to consider the competition between the kinetic energy of the gauge field and the potential energy of the scalar field. By varying the parameters of the model, such as the coupling constants and the lattice spacing, we can investigate the different phases that the system can exhibit.

One of the key phases in the phase diagram of the Abelian-Higgs model is the Higgs phase, where the gauge field acquires a mass due to the spontaneous breaking of gauge symmetry by the scalar field. In this phase, the system exhibits long-range order and behaves like a superconductor.

Another important phase is the confinement phase, where the gauge field is confined and cannot propagate freely. This phase is characterized by the absence of long-range order and is relevant for understanding the behavior of quark-gluon plasma in high-energy physics.

By studying the phase diagram of the Abelian-Higgs model in 1+1D on a lattice, we can gain valuable insights into the underlying physics of the system and better understand the behavior of complex systems in condensed matter physics.

Through our analysis, we aim to elucidate the various ways in which the spins respond to the quench and how they subsequently evolve over time. The study of neutrino oscillations has greatly advanced our understanding of these elusive particles. Solar neutrinos, which are produced by nuclear reactions in the Sun's core, were the first to provide evidence for neutrino oscillations. Atmospheric neutrinos, originating from cosmic ray interactions in the Earth's atmosphere, also exhibit oscillatory behavior. Supernova neutrinos, released during the explosive death of massive stars, further showcase the phenomenon of oscillations.

In laboratory settings, scientists have successfully recreated neutrino oscillations using particle accelerators and reactors. By comparing the results from oscillation experiments with the search for neutrinoless double beta decay, scientists can probe the fundamental properties of neutrinos and potentially unlock new physics beyond the Standard Model.

In conclusion, the interplay between solar, atmospheric, supernova, and laboratory neutrino oscillations, along with investigations into neutrinoless double beta decay, represents a fascinating field of research that continues to push the boundaries of our understanding of particle physics.

Neutron stars are some of the densest and most mysterious objects in the universe. They form through the violent processes of collapsing massive stars or the merging of compact objects such as white dwarfs. When these events occur, they release huge amounts of energy and material, resulting in bright transients that can be observed by telescopes here on Earth.

The collapse of a massive star occurs when the core runs out of fuel to sustain nuclear fusion. The outer layers of the star will be expelled in a powerful explosion called a supernova, while the core collapses down to become a neutron star. This process releases an immense amount of energy, causing the bright transients we can detect.

Similarly, when two compact objects like neutron stars or black holes merge, they produce an even more energetic event. The intense gravitational forces involved in such a merger release gravitational waves, gamma-ray bursts, and other electromagnetic radiation that can be observed across the universe.

Studying these bright transients is crucial for understanding the formation and behavior of neutron stars. By analyzing the characteristics of the emitted light, astronomers can learn more about the physical properties of these exotic objects. Neutron stars play a significant role in the evolution of galaxies and the cosmos as a whole, making them a fascinating topic of research in the field of astrophysics.

Phase transitions at finite temperatures are a crucial aspect of understanding the behavior of systems governed by the Bose-Fermi-Hubbard model. In this study, the self-consistent random phase approximation method is employed to delve deeper into these transitions and gain insights into the system's dynamics.

The Bose-Fermi-Hubbard model is a theoretical framework that describes the interplay between bosonic and fermionic particles in a lattice structure, where interactions between particles play a significant role in determining the system's behavior. By exploring the relationship between these two concepts, we can gain deeper insights into the underlying mechanisms governing the behavior of quantum systems and how they can be optimized for diverse applications. For instance, a more complex quantum circuit may require stronger error correction capabilities to ensure the reliability of quantum computations. Conversely, efficient error correction techniques can reduce the overall complexity of quantum circuits, leading to more streamlined and efficient quantum algorithms.

Understanding the interplay between quantum circuit complexity and AQEC capability is essential for advancing the field of quantum information science and harnessing the full potential of quantum technologies. By leveraging this connection, we can design more robust quantum algorithms, improve error correction strategies, and pave the way for practical implementations of quantum computers in various fields, from cryptography to materials science. Ultimately, this research not only deepens our theoretical understanding of quantum systems but also accelerates the development of real-world applications that leverage the power of quantum mechanics.

For a body with negligible mass moving in the gravitational field of a star and one planet in a circular orbit (the circular restricted three-body problem), five equilibrium points exist. These points are crucial in understanding the dynamics of the system. The first three equilibrium points, known as L1, L2, and L3, lie along the line connecting the center of mass of the star-planet system. L1 is located between the star and the planet, where the gravitational pull of the two bodies balances out to keep the smaller body in a fixed position relative to the planet. L2 is located on the opposite side of the planet, while L3 is on the line passing through the center of mass but on the opposite side of the star. These points are often referred to as unstable equilibrium points, meaning any small perturbation will cause the body to drift away from its position.

The remaining two equilibrium points, L4 and L5, are known as the triangular equilibrium points. They form an equilateral triangle with the star and the planet, located 60 degrees ahead and behind the planet in its orbit. These points are stable equilibrium points, meaning that any small disturbances will cause the body to oscillate around the point rather than drift away. L4 and L5 are particularly interesting as they represent unique regions where the gravitational forces of the star and planet combine in such a way that a third body could theoretically orbit in sync with the planet without being disturbed.

In conclusion, the existence of these equilibrium points in the circular restricted three-body problem significantly impacts the dynamics of the system and opens up possibilities for the study of celestial mechanics in complex gravitational interactions.

The global spin alignment of vector mesons provides valuable insights into the dynamics of the vorticity field in non-central relativistic heavy-ion collisions. This phenomenon offers a unique opportunity to investigate the angular momentum distribution within the created quark-gluon plasma (QGP) and understand its formation and evolution.

In non-central collisions, the initial state of the system is characterized by a non-zero impact parameter, leading to the development of a strong vorticity field. This vorticity can imprint its signature on the spin alignment of vector mesons produced in the collision, enabling researchers to indirectly probe the properties of the QGP medium.

The study of spin alignment in vector mesons offers a new perspective on the thermalization process and the hydrodynamic evolution of the QGP. By analyzing the polarization patterns of vector mesons, researchers can gain valuable information about the angular momentum transport and the collective flow of the system.

Moreover, the global spin alignment of vector mesons can also serve as a sensitive probe for investigating the possible violation of local parity and charge-conjugation (P and C) symmetries in the QGP. By studying the azimuthal angular correlations of vector meson decay products, scientists can explore the interplay between vorticity, magnetic fields, and chiral magnetic effects in the QGP.

Overall, the global spin alignment of vector mesons is a powerful tool that enhances our understanding of the complex dynamics of relativistic heavy-ion collisions and provides crucial insights into the properties of the quark-gluon plasma.

The multi-marginal partial optimal transport (POT) problem is an area of research that focuses on finding the optimal transport plan between multiple discrete measures that may not have the same number of supports. In this problem, we are dealing with $m$ measures, each with at most $n$ supports. These measures may have different weights assigned to each support, making them unbalanced.

The goal of solving the POT problem is to determine how to redistribute the mass from the supports of the input measures to minimize the overall cost of transporting the mass. This can be a complex problem due to the different weights and the varying number of supports in each measure.

Researchers in this field employ mathematical optimization techniques to find the optimal transport plan that minimizes the cost function while satisfying certain constraints. These constraints may include ensuring that the total mass is conserved during the transport process or enforcing bounds on the amount of mass that can be transported between certain supports.

By studying the multi-marginal partial optimal transport problem, researchers gain insights into how to efficiently redistribute mass between multiple measures with different characteristics. This research has applications in various fields such as image processing, machine learning, and economics, where the efficient transport of resources is crucial for optimal outcomes.

For a transcendental real number $ \zeta $, let us delve into the study of the classical Diophantine exponents $ w_{n}( \zeta)$ and $ \widehat{w}_{n}( \zeta)$. These exponents play a crucial role in number theory and have significant theoretical implications.

The Diophantine exponent $ w_{n}( \zeta)$ is defined as the infimum of all real numbers $ w $ such that the inequality $ | \zeta - \frac{p}{q} | < \frac{1}{q^{w}} $ has infinitely many solutions in coprime integers $ p $ and $ q $ with $ q>0 $ and $ q \leq n $. This concept is fundamental in approximating transcendental numbers by rational approximations and is essential for understanding the distribution of such numbers along the real line.

On the other hand, the Diophantine exponent $ \widehat{w}_{n}( \zeta)$ is a related quantity that considers the distribution of the fractional parts of the numbers $ q \zeta $ for coprime integers $ p $ and $ q $ with $ q>0 $ and $ q \leq n $. This exponent gives insights into the equidistribution properties of the fractional parts of multiples of $ \zeta $.

Overall, the study of these classical Diophantine exponents opens up a fascinating realm of exploration in number theory, providing deep insights into the nature of transcendental real numbers and their approximations by rational numbers.

The Sivers function, named after physicist Daniele Sivers, is a fundamental quantity in understanding the structure of the proton. It plays a crucial role in our understanding of how quarks and gluons are distributed within the proton and how their motion and spin contribute to its overall properties.

The Sivers function is defined in terms of a correlation between the transverse spin of the proton and the transverse momentum of its quarks during a high-energy collision. This asymmetry provides valuable insight into the dynamics of the strong force and the mechanisms governing the internal structure of the proton.

HERMES (HERA Measurements of Spin) is an experiment conducted at the HERA electron-proton collider in Germany, focusing on studying the spin structure of the proton using polarized electron and proton beams. Through analyzing single spin asymmetries in semi-inclusive deeply inelastic scattering processes, HERMES has provided crucial data that has enabled the extraction of the Sivers function.

The data from HERMES has not only validated the existence of the Sivers function but has also provided essential constraints on its behavior. This information has advanced our understanding of the underlying principles of Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) and has contributed significantly to the field of hadron physics.

Overall, the extraction of the Sivers function from HERMES data has been a significant milestone in unraveling the complex dynamics of the proton's internal structure and shedding light on the fundamental interactions governing the behavior of quarks and gluons within this fundamental particle.

In DC microgrids with constant power terminals, managing power flow is crucial for maintaining system stability and efficiency. This is because the power flow problem in such systems is non-linear in nature, meaning it cannot be easily solved using traditional linear methods. Instead, a more advanced technique such as Newton's method is required to accurately compute power flow values.

Newton's method is an iterative numerical technique that calculates the root of a non-linear equation by approximating it as a straight line. In the context of power flow analysis in DC microgrids, Newton's method is used to iteratively solve the system of non-linear power flow equations until convergence is achieved. This process involves updating the power flow variables at each iteration based on the calculated error until the solution converges to a stable state.

By using Newton's method to solve the power flow problem in DC microgrids with constant power terminals, system operators can accurately determine the power flow values at different nodes and ensure that the system operates within safe limits. This information is essential for making informed decisions about system operation, control, and protection strategies to prevent overloads and voltage instabilities.

In summary, the application of Newton's method in solving the non-linear power flow problem in DC microgrids with constant power terminals is crucial for ensuring system reliability and stability. Its effectiveness lies in its ability to accurately compute power flow values and provide valuable insights for system operators to make informed decisions for optimal system operation.

Software quality plays a critical role in ensuring the security of applications and systems. Poor software quality can result in vulnerabilities that can be exploited by malicious actors, leading to security breaches and data leaks. In addition, poor software quality can also lead to performance issues and system failures, further impacting the overall security of an application. To mitigate the risks associated with poor software quality, it is crucial for organizations to prioritize security in the software development lifecycle. This includes implementing secure coding practices, conducting regular security audits, and embracing a culture of security awareness among developers and stakeholders. By investing in software quality assurance and security measures, organizations can enhance the resilience of their applications and protect sensitive data from potential breaches.

The muon g-2 anomaly refers to the discrepancy between the measured value of the magnetic moment of the muon and the value predicted by the Standard Model of particle physics. This anomaly has garnered significant interest in the physics community as it could potentially signal the presence of new particles or interactions beyond what is currently understood.

One possible explanation for the muon g-2 anomaly lies in models with extended Higgs and matter sectors. In these models, additional Higgs fields and new particles are introduced to the Standard Model, providing new sources of contributions to the muon's magnetic moment. By incorporating these extensions, it may be possible to reconcile the experimental data with theoretical predictions.

One particular framework that has been explored in the context of the muon g-2 anomaly is the two Higgs doublet model. This model introduces an additional Higgs doublet to the Standard Model, leading to new interactions that can influence the muon's magnetic moment. By investigating the implications of this extended Higgs sector on the anomaly, researchers have been able to elucidate potential mechanisms for resolving the discrepancy.

Overall, probing extensions of the Standard Model, such as the two Higgs doublet model, offers a promising avenue for addressing the muon g-2 anomaly and probing the frontiers of particle physics. Further theoretical and experimental investigations in this direction may shed light on the nature of the anomaly and potentially pave the way for new physics beyond the Standard Model.

Quadratic solitons, also known as quadratic spatial solitons, are characterized by their self-trapped, localized beams of light that propagate without changing their shape due to a balance between diffraction and nonlinearity. These solitons have been extensively studied in the field of nonlinear optics and have been shown to exhibit interesting properties such as self-focusing and self-phase modulation.

One fascinating finding in recent research is the equivalence between quadratic solitons and solitons in a nonlocal Kerr medium. The nonlocal Kerr medium is a theoretical model used to describe the behavior of light in a nonlinear medium where the refractive index varies as a function of the light intensity. Remarkably, it has been demonstrated that the dynamics of solitons in a nonlocal Kerr medium closely resemble the behavior of quadratic solitons, despite the different nature of the two systems.

This discovery has significant implications for the understanding of soliton dynamics and the development of optical devices based on soliton interactions. By establishing a connection between quadratic solitons and solitons in a nonlocal Kerr medium, researchers can leverage the insights gained from studying one system to understand the behavior of the other. This cross-fertilization of concepts and ideas has the potential to open up new avenues for the manipulation and control of light beams in various optical systems, leading to advancements in fields such as telecommunications, laser technology, and optical computing.

Through the application of advanced mathematical techniques like the Perturbative Least Action Method, we seek to deepen our knowledge of the intricate interplay between cosmological parameters and the behavior of galactic structures within the Local Group.

These groups exhibit fascinating properties and play a crucial role in various mathematical applications, including combinatorics, representation theory, and algebraic geometry.

The determinant of irreducible representations serves as a fundamental concept in the representation theory of groups. By exploring the determinants of irreducible representations within the framework of $\mathbb{Z}_r \wr S_n$, we aim to deepen our understanding of the intricate relationships between these mathematical structures.

This research is essential in unraveling the intricate algebraic and geometric properties of these groups and shedding light on their significance in various mathematical contexts.

By shedding light on the determinant of irreducible representations in the context of $\mathbb{Z}_r \wr S_n$, this paper contributes to the broader field of mathematics and provides valuable insights for further exploration and research in this area.

Let $G$ be a multiplicative subgroup of $\mathbb{Q}_p$. This means that $G$ is a subset of the $p$-adic numbers $\mathbb{Q}_p$ under multiplication that is closed under the operation of multiplication. In other words, if $a$ and $b$ are elements of $G$, then their product $ab$ must also be an element of $G$.

The $p$-adic numbers $\mathbb{Q}_p$ are an extension of the rational numbers $\mathbb{Q}$ that provide a complete and metric space with respect to the $p$-adic norm. The $p$-adic norm on $\mathbb{Q}_p$ is defined as $|x|_p = p^{-v_p(x)}$, where $v_p(x)$ denotes the $p$-adic valuation of $x$. This norm is non-archimedean, meaning that the triangle inequality is replaced by a stronger inequality: $|x+y|_p \leq \max\{|x|_p, |y|_p\}$.

Multiplicative subgroups of $\mathbb{Q}_p$ play an important role in number theory and arithmetic geometry. They are used to study various algebraic and arithmetic properties of $p$-adic fields, such as divisibility, factorization, and the structure of units in the ring of $p$-adic integers.

In summary, a multiplicative subgroup $G$ of $\mathbb{Q}_p$ consists of elements that can be multiplied together within the $p$-adic number system, and these subgroups are instrumental in understanding the algebraic and arithmetic properties of $p$-adic fields.

In our research, we are investigating the phenomenon of carrier concentration bistabilities that arise in highly photo-excited electron gases. As the photo-excitation level increases, the electron gas can exhibit bistable behavior, where it can exist in multiple stable states depending on the initial conditions. This bistable nature is a result of the complex interplay between the different processes occurring within the electron gas.

By studying these carrier concentration bistabilities, we aim to gain a better understanding of the behavior of highly photo-excited electron gases and explore their potential applications in optoelectronic devices. This research has implications for the development of new materials and technologies that rely on the unique properties of non-equilibrium electron gases.

Overall, our work contributes to the field of semiconductor physics and sheds light on the rich dynamics that can emerge in highly excited electron systems. By delving into the intricacies of carrier concentration bistabilities, we hope to uncover new insights that can drive progress in the field of optoelectronics and advanced semiconductor devices.

The complexity assessment of a classification problem plays a crucial role in determining the most suitable algorithm to use for solving it. Different classification problems may vary in terms of their complexity due to factors such as the number of classes, size of the dataset, and the distribution of the data. By understanding the complexity of a classification problem, data scientists can make informed decisions on the most effective approach to take.

One aspect of complexity assessment is measuring the separability of classes within the dataset. If the classes are well-separated, it indicates a less complex classification problem, and simpler algorithms like logistic regression or decision trees may suffice. However, if the classes overlap significantly, more advanced algorithms like support vector machines or neural networks may be needed to accurately classify the data.

Moreover, the dimensionality of the dataset also contributes to the complexity of the classification problem. High-dimensional data requires more complex models to capture the relationships between features accurately, which can increase the computational cost and potential for overfitting.

In conclusion, understanding the complexity of a classification problem is essential for selecting the most suitable algorithm, optimizing model performance, and avoiding potential pitfalls. By assessing factors such as class separability and dataset dimensionality, data scientists can effectively navigate the challenges posed by different classification problems and achieve accurate predictive models.

Overall, the development of efficient and controllable RF sources for superconducting accelerators is crucial for pushing the boundaries of particle physics research. With advancements in RF technology, we are able to create accelerators capable of generating high-energy beams with unprecedented power levels, opening up new possibilities for scientific discovery and exploration.

By utilizing fractionalized degrees of freedom, we are able to capture the unique properties of antiferromagnetic magnons in this specific configuration. This approach not only provides valuable insights into the behavior of magnons in Néel states but also sheds light on the broader connection between quantum spin liquids and antiferromagnetism.

Our methodology involves a careful analysis of the interactions between magnons and their surrounding lattice, taking into account the fractional nature of the degrees of freedom involved. By incorporating these unconventional variables, we are able to construct a more comprehensive and accurate description of the dynamics of antiferromagnetic magnons on a bipartite lattice in the Néel state.

Overall, our work contributes to the growing body of research exploring the interplay between fractionalized degrees of freedom, quantum spin liquids, and antiferromagnetism. By pushing the boundaries of traditional theoretical frameworks, we hope to deepen our understanding of the complex behaviors exhibited by magnetic systems in condensed matter physics.

We offer a novel geometric interpretation of the annihilation range in reactions such as $ \bar{p}p \rightarrow$ {em two light mesons}. This interpretation relies on the understanding of Lorentz effects in particle reactions.

In particle physics, annihilation refers to the process in which a particle and its antiparticle collide and are converted into other particles. The annihilation range is the distance at which this collision occurs and is a key parameter in understanding the dynamics of these reactions.

By incorporating Lorentz effects into our interpretation, we can visualize the annihilation range as a region in spacetime where the energies and momenta of the colliding particles interact to produce the final state particles. Lorentz transformations play a crucial role in relating the coordinates of this region in different reference frames, allowing us to fully grasp the complex interplay of forces and energies involved in the annihilation process.

This geometric approach provides a visually intuitive way to comprehend the intricate nature of particle collisions and offers new insights into the underlying physics at play. By exploring the annihilation range from this perspective, researchers can enhance their understanding of these reactions and potentially uncover new avenues for further research in particle physics.

By capturing high-resolution images of star clusters in distant galaxies, astronomers can gain valuable insights into the complex processes that govern the creation of stars and galaxies. Lie superalgebras are a rich area of study in mathematics, specifically in the realm of algebra. In this particular research project, we delve into the concept of direct limits of finite-dimensional basic classical simple Lie superalgebras. By exploring these limits, we aim to gather insights into the structure and properties of these Lie superalgebras.

One of the key aspects we investigate in this study is the conjugacy classes of Cartan subalgebras under the group of automorphisms. The Cartan subalgebra plays a crucial role in the study of Lie superalgebras as it allows for the decomposition of the Lie superalgebra into simpler components. By understanding the conjugacy classes of Cartan subalgebras, we gain a deeper understanding of the symmetries and transformations within these Lie superalgebras.

Through our research, we hope to uncover new connections and relationships within the realm of finite-dimensional basic classical simple Lie superalgebras. By shedding light on the direct limits and conjugacy classes of Cartan subalgebras, we aim to contribute to the broader mathematical community's understanding of these intricate and fascinating structures.

Overall, this work represents a step towards a more comprehensive and nuanced understanding of Lie superalgebras, paving the way for further exploration and discovery in this exciting field of mathematics.

Overall, the approach of predicting body joint coordinates relative to the hip joint offers a robust and effective way to estimate 3D human poses. By leveraging the hip joint as a central point of reference, this method improves accuracy, consistency, and reliability in the estimation process, making it a valuable tool in various fields including biomechanics, computer vision, robotics, and virtual reality.

In the study of $(\alpha, \beta)$-metrics, various curvature properties play a crucial role in understanding the geometric properties of the space. In this paper, we investigate a specific condition on these metrics that allows us to establish an equivalence between three important curvature notions: isotropic S-curvature, weakly isotropic S-curvature, and isotropic mean Berwald curvature.

Isotropic S-curvature measures the deviation of a curve from being isotropic, which signifies the uniformity of the curvature along the curve. Weakly isotropic S-curvature relaxes the isotropic condition by allowing for small deviations from isotropy. On the other hand, isotropic mean Berwald curvature captures the average variation of curvature over a curve segment.

Our findings reveal that there exists a condition on $(\alpha, \beta)$-metrics that ensures these three curvature properties are interchangeable. This result provides a deeper insight into the intrinsic geometry of the space described by these metrics and sheds light on the relationships between different curvature measures.

By establishing this equivalence, we not only enhance our understanding of the geometric structures of $(\alpha, \beta)$-metrics but also pave the way for further research in the field. The implications of this result extend to various applications in differential geometry, optimization, and theoretical physics, making it a significant contribution to the mathematical community.
